children: By Rob Curran
U.S. stocks surged as oil prices tumbled and traders bet a divided government would be good for business, offsetting unease about artificial-intelligence bets.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 1569.40 points, or 3.03%, to 53356.12, its biggest gain since April 9, 2025. The S&P 500 rose 119.70 points, or 1.58%, to 7688.62 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose 364.50 points, or 1.44%, to 25736.51.

A slew of seat gains in the Senate and House of Representatives gave the Democratic party a dominant position in Congress. Investors wagered that President Trump and the congressional Democrats would be deadlocked on most issues, diminishing the risk of new regulations.

Stocks and Treasury bonds were also buoyed by a plunge in the price of oil as traders bet that comments from President Trump and Vice President Vance about the unpopularity of the Iran war foreshadowed an exit for U.S. troops from the Middle East.
Oil futures plummeted $7.97, or 8.3% to $88.12 a barrel in New York, completing the largest three-session percentage retreat in almost five years.

The yield on the policy-sensitive two-year Treasury fell 0.033 percentage point to 4.579%. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note dropped 0.060 percentage point to 4.891%. The yield on the 30-year bond fell 0.043 percentage point to 5.280%.
The U.S. dollar slipped against major rivals as traders weighed the implications of the retreat in oil prices for Federal Reserve monetary policy.
Dollar-sensitive gold futures gained $133.20, or 3.4% to $4061.10 a troy ounce.

It was a broad stock-market rally, with most sectors rising by 2% or more. Below the surface there were indications of nervousness about the potential for regulation of AI and how that could compound existing bubble fears. Hyperscalers and "neocloud" companies have borrowed hand over fist to fund their AI ambitions. Any sign congressional Democrats or state officials are tapping the brakes on data-center development may dim the outlook for AI profits, and make those loans harder to pay back.
One brokerage said the AI trade could remain intact under the large incoming class of Democratic governors.

"Polling has found that the most politically popular approach on data centers mirrors Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's position: build data centers, but with community engagement and while keeping prices down," Jefferies' strategists said in a note to clients. "We expect Democratic governors to adopt similar guardrails, which should mute the backlash over time."
Shares of some neocloud and data-center developers resumed their decline.

CoreWeave was off by 9.9% to $48.42, and shares are now down by 32% year to date. Hut 8 shares slid 23% to $48.94 after the Miami data-center developer posted a $277.4 million operating loss for the third quarter.
Shares of monitoring and cybersecurity software maker Datadog slid 14% to $188.72 after it said their largest customer--an undisclosed AI company--cut back on usage.
Chip maker Advanced Micro Devices ticked up 1% to $488.78 after reporting a jump in demand for its AI-enabling GPU chips.

Consumer companies gained as the plunge in oil prices boosted expectations for an easing of inflationary pressures. The SPDR Home Builders exchange-traded fund added 5.4% to $107.52. Home-improvement retailer Lowe's rose 7.5% to $229.38, one of its biggest percentage gains in recent years.

Consumer-facing tech companies also advanced with shares of Amazon up 6.1% to $266.03 on hopes that lower fuel prices would spur holiday-season spending. Apple added 5.3% to $349.51. Uber Technologies' shares rose 4.9% to $69.87 after the company said as part of its third-quarter earnings release that higher fuel prices hampered its ability to meet demand in markets such as India and Brazil.

In another positive sign for economic activity, W.W. Grainger's shares rose 6.5% to $1489.39 after the Chicago distributor of tools, plumbing gear and other equipment posted robust revenue growth and boosted its growth projection for the year.
McDonald's shares rose 6.5% to $280.22 after the biggest restaurant chain in the country logged quarterly earnings growth, as strong international demand offset sluggish U.S. sales.
